questions.question: Which part of a specification states what must be true of the result after the function has run?
options: Purpose
Precondition
Postcondition
The type signature
questions.explanation: Purpose is the one-sentence summary, precondition constrains the arguments before the call, and postcondition constrains the result afterwards. The type signature says what shape the answer has, not what value it must be.
optionFeedback: Purpose is the one-sentence summary of what the function represents, not a constraint on the result.
Precondition constrains the arguments before the function runs, not the result afterwards.
Correct. The postcondition is exactly the assertion that must hold of the result once the function returns.
A type signature (e.g. Char -> Bool) restricts what shape the result has, but says nothing about which value of that shape is correct — that is the postcondition's job.

questions.question: isDigit c = ('0' <= c) && (c <= '9'). What does isDigit '/' evaluate to, and why?
options: True, because '/' is next to '0' on a keyboard
False, because '/' has a character code one less than '0', so '0' <= '/' is False
False, because '&&' always returns False for punctuation
It is a type error, because '/' is not a digit
questions.explanation: '/' (code 47) comes immediately before '0' (code 48) in character order, so '0' <= '/' is False, the && short-circuits, and the whole expression is False. This is exactly the boundary case Chapter 4's isDigitChar discussion cared about.
optionFeedback: Keyboard adjacency is irrelevant — comparison operators on Char compare character codes, not physical key layout.
Correct — '/' sits one code point below '0', so the first comparison already fails.
&& is ordinary boolean AND; it does not treat punctuation specially. It returns False here because one operand is False, not because of the character class.
Char is Char regardless of what it represents — comparing '/' against '0' and '9' type checks fine and simply evaluates to False.

questions.question: For fac :: Integer -> Integer with the mathematical factorial specification, which set does -1 belong to?
options: Iv, because -1 is a legal Integer
Ie, because the precondition restricts the domain to non-negative integers
Ov, because fac must return something
Oe, because -1 is negative
questions.explanation: Iv and Ie partition the *input* set I. -1 type checks as an Integer (so it is in I), but it fails the precondition n >= 0, so it belongs to Ie, not Iv. Oe is about outputs, and is a separate question from where -1 sits as an input.
optionFeedback: Iv is the valid-input subset, defined by the precondition, not by the type. -1 satisfies the type but fails n >= 0.
Correct. -1 is a legal Integer (so it's in I) but violates the precondition, which is exactly the definition of Ie.
Ov and Oe classify outputs, not inputs. -1 is an argument, so the question is about Iv vs Ie.
Being negative is why it lands in Ie — but Oe is the wrong set name, because -1 is an input, not an output.

questions.question: Why is it useful to say a type is 'usually wider than Iv' rather than just relying on the type signature?
options: It isn't useful — the type signature already captures every constraint on the arguments
Because the type only rules out ill-typed arguments; the precondition rules out further ones that are well-typed but mathematically invalid, and the compiler cannot see that gap
Because Haskell's type checker is unreliable for Integer arguments
Because Iv and the type are always identical for total functions
questions.explanation: Integer -> Integer admits every integer, including negative ones. The precondition n >= 0 is a further, semantic restriction that GHC's type checker cannot enforce — it can only check that -1 has the right type, not that it satisfies the intended domain. That gap is exactly where unguarded recursion or partial functions fail.
optionFeedback: It is useful precisely because the type signature under-constrains the domain — Integer accepts -1 just as happily as 5.
Correct — this is the same gap Chapter 5 met when fac (-1) looped: type-valid but precondition-invalid.
GHC's type checker is completely reliable here; the issue is that a semantic precondition (n >= 0) isn't something a type system this simple can express.
They coincide only when the precondition is 'accept every value of the type' — which is the exception, not the rule, for a function with any real domain restriction.

questions.question: Which mechanism converts an out-of-precondition argument into a value that is visible in the type, forcing the caller to handle it?
options: error "..."
Extending the base case
Returning Maybe
Adding a type annotation
questions.explanation: Returning Maybe reports failure as data (Nothing), which appears in the function's type and which the caller must pattern-match on or otherwise handle. error stops the program; extending the base case gives the out-of-range value a documented answer instead of treating it as invalid at all.
optionFeedback: error "..." rejects the argument by crashing — the failure is not visible in the type, and there is nothing for the caller to handle except a runtime exception.
Extending the base case redefines what 'valid' means (it defines the value), rather than reporting a failure the caller has to deal with.
Correct. Maybe puts the possibility of failure directly into the return type, which the type checker then forces every caller to handle.
A type annotation only pins down which type GHC should infer for an ambiguous expression — it does not change how a precondition violation is handled.

questions.question: In facMaybe, what does fmap (n *) (facMaybe (n - 1)) evaluate to when facMaybe (n - 1) is Nothing?
options: Nothing
Just (n * 0)
It throws a runtime exception
Just n
questions.explanation: fmap f Nothing = Nothing, by definition of fmap for Maybe. There is no value inside Nothing for (n *) to be applied to, so the failure simply propagates unchanged — n is never multiplied by anything.
optionFeedback: Correct. fmap's second equation, fmap f Nothing = Nothing, means the failure passes through untouched.
This would require treating the missing value as 0, but fmap never invents a value to apply f to — it leaves Nothing exactly as Nothing.
facMaybe never calls error or an unguarded partial function on this path, so there is nothing to throw — the whole point of using Maybe here is to avoid a runtime exception.
Just n would mean (n *) was never applied at all while still wrapping in Just — but fmap on Nothing produces Nothing, not a Just of anything.

questions.question: What is Iv for facMaybe :: Integer -> Maybe Integer, given that it reports failure via Nothing rather than rejecting it?
options: The non-negative integers only
The empty set — no input is ever truly valid
Every Integer, because there is no longer an argument the function refuses to accept
Only 0 and 1, the base cases
questions.explanation: Reporting failure through the return type (Maybe) is precisely what removes the restriction on the input side: facMaybe accepts every Integer and always terminates with some Maybe Integer, valid or not. The 'invalid' case now shows up in Ov/Oe territory (as Nothing) rather than in Iv/Ie.
optionFeedback: That was Iv for the error-based fac, which does reject negative arguments. facMaybe's whole design point is to accept them instead and report failure through the type.
The set is not empty — facMaybe successfully returns Just k for every non-negative input, and Nothing (a defined result) for negative ones.
Correct. Once failure is reported rather than rejected, every Integer is a valid argument; the distinction between success and failure moves to the output (Just vs Nothing).
0 and 1 are only the base cases of the recursion, not a restriction on which arguments facMaybe will accept.

questions.question: fac 0 = 0 type checks without error. Is it correct?
options: Yes, because it type checks and GHC accepted it
No — it is well-typed but violates the postcondition (0! = 1, not 0), so it fails against the specification
The question is meaningless without running the tests first
Yes, because fac 0 terminates
questions.explanation: Type checking only confirms that Integer -> Integer is used consistently. It says nothing about whether the value returned is the one the specification promises. The postcondition for fac requires fac 0 = 1 (the base case of factorial), so fac 0 = 0 is well-typed and wrong.
optionFeedback: Type checking is a necessary but not sufficient condition for correctness — this is exactly the point the lesson makes with this example.
Correct. It compiles fine (consistent types) but breaks the postcondition, which is the actual standard for correctness.
Testing gives evidence either way, but you don't need to run anything here — the postcondition already tells you 0! = 1, so fac 0 = 0 is wrong by inspection.
Termination is one requirement for correctness, but it is not sufficient on its own — the result must also satisfy the postcondition, and 0 does not.

questions.question: Why is 'this code is correct' (with no further qualification) an incomplete claim?
options: Because Haskell code can never be proven correct under any circumstances
Because correctness is only ever defined relative to a stated specification — the same code can be correct against one specification and wrong against another
Because only compiled languages can have correct code
Because correctness only applies to functions with no arguments
questions.explanation: Section 4 states this directly: there is no such thing as correct code in the abstract. Correctness is always 'correct with respect to' some stated purpose, precondition, and postcondition. Change the specification, and the same unchanged code can become incorrect.
optionFeedback: Proof by induction (Lesson 2) does establish correctness for many definitions — the claim in this lesson is narrower: correctness is always relative to something, not that it's unattainable.
Correct — 'correct' is a two-place relation between code and a specification, not a one-place property of code alone.
Correctness-relative-to-a-specification applies regardless of whether the language is compiled or interpreted; it's a property of the code/specification pair.
The claim applies to every function, regardless of arity — a zero-argument function still needs a stated postcondition to be judged against.

questions.question: What, precisely, does 'cohesion' mean for a function, as this section uses the term?
options: A function should be as short as possible, measured in lines of code
A function should do one and only one logical task — focus on what is computed, and let composition combine small, single-purpose functions rather than folding several tasks into one definition
A function should never call any other function
A function should always return a String, since that is the most flexible output type
questions.explanation: Cohesion is about the number of logical jobs a function does, not its length or whether it calls other functions. reportAverage is short and calls nothing external, yet it still bundles two tasks (computing and formatting) into one definition — exactly the thing cohesion says to avoid.
optionFeedback: reportAverage is actually the shorter of the two versions by line count, yet it is the one criticised — brevity is not what cohesion measures.
Correct — cohesion asks whether a function has exactly one logical job; average and report are each cohesive on their own, while reportAverage folds both jobs into one.
average and report each call other functions freely (sum, fromIntegral, show, ++); calling other functions is not what cohesion restricts.
String is the return type of report and reportAverage, but average deliberately returns a Double instead — cohesion is about task count, not about preferring any particular result type.

questions.question: Why is average :: [Double] -> Double preferred over reportAverage :: [Double] -> String, given they compute related results?
options: average runs faster because it skips string formatting
average can be tested against a numeric postcondition and reused wherever a Double is needed, while reportAverage bundles two tasks into one and can only be tested by string comparison
reportAverage is invalid Haskell
There is no real difference — both are equally reusable
questions.explanation: This is the cohesion argument from Section 5: splitting 'compute' from 'format as a report' gives each function a single, testable, reusable job. Performance is not the point being made here.
optionFeedback: Performance is not the reason given in the lesson — string formatting is cheap relative to summing a list either way. The reason is testability and reuse.
Correct. average has a clean numeric postcondition and can be composed into other calculations; reportAverage conflates 'compute' and 'format' so it can only be checked and reused as a whole string.
reportAverage compiles and runs fine — the criticism is about design (cohesion), not validity.
They differ exactly in reusability: average can feed any further Double-consuming function, reportAverage's output is locked into a specific string shape.

questions.question: average has the precondition 'the list is non-empty'. Which of these guarantees average . f is safe, for every list argument to f?
options: f's postcondition guarantees f never returns an empty list
f's precondition matches average's precondition
f and average have the same argument type, [Double]
average is total, so the precondition doesn't matter
questions.explanation: Composing g after f (here, average after f) is safe when f's postcondition guarantees g's precondition. average needs a non-empty list, so f must be guaranteed to never hand it an empty one — that is a statement about f's postcondition, not its precondition or its argument type.
optionFeedback: Correct. The rule is: the postcondition of the earlier function (f) must guarantee the precondition of the later one (average) — exactly f promising 'never an empty list.'
f's own precondition is about what f accepts, not about what f hands to average — matching preconditions doesn't say anything about f's output.
Matching argument types only makes the composition type check; it says nothing about whether average's non-empty precondition is respected.
average is not total — it fails (NaN, or an exception if you switch to Maybe) on an empty list, which is exactly why the precondition matters.
